solution:
Diagonal matrices add and subtract entry by entry along the diagonal, so work with the three diagonal entries separately.
\(B + C - A = \text{diag}\,[\,4 + (-3) - 2,\ \ -6 + 4 - (-3),\ \ -3 + 1 - (-5)\,]\)
\(= \text{diag}\,[-1\ \ 1\ \ 3]\)
Hence \(B + C - A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \text{diag}\,[-1\ \ 1\ \ 3]\)

Scalar multiples of a diagonal matrix are again diagonal, so combine the corresponding diagonal entries.
\(2A + B - 5C = \text{diag}\,[\,2(2) + 4 - 5(-3),\ \ 2(-3) + (-6) - 5(4),\ \ 2(-5) + (-3) - 5(1)\,]\)
\(= \text{diag}\,[\,4 + 4 + 15,\ \ -6 - 6 - 20,\ \ -10 - 3 - 5\,]\)
Hence \(2A + B - 5C = \text{diag}\,[23\ \ -32\ \ -18]\)

Replace \(\alpha\) by \(-\alpha\) throughout and use \(\cos(-\alpha) = \cos\alpha\), \(\sin(-\alpha) = -\sin\alpha\).
The entry \(-\sin\alpha\) becomes \(-\sin(-\alpha) = \sin\alpha\) and the entry \(\sin\alpha\) becomes \(-\sin\alpha\), while the cosines are unchanged.
\(f(-\alpha) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\alpha & \sin\alpha & 0 \\ -\sin\alpha & \cos\alpha & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)

Add \(f(-\alpha)\) from part (i) to \(f(\alpha)\) entry by entry; the two sine terms in each off-diagonal position are negatives of each other and cancel.
\(f(-\alpha) + f(\alpha) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\alpha + \cos\alpha & \sin\alpha - \sin\alpha & 0 \\ -\sin\alpha + \sin\alpha & \cos\alpha + \cos\alpha & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 + 1 \end{bmatrix}\)
Hence \(f(-\alpha) + f(\alpha) = \begin{bmatrix} 2\cos\alpha & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\cos\alpha & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\)

Write \(M = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), so the two equations are \(2A - B = M\) ... (1) and \(A + 3B = M\) ... (2).
To eliminate \(A\), form \(2 \times (2) - (1)\):
\((2A + 6B) - (2A - B) = 2M - M\), that is \(7B = M\), so \(B = \dfrac{1}{7}M = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{7} & -\dfrac{1}{7} \\ 0 & \dfrac{1}{7} \end{bmatrix}\).
Substituting in (2): \(A = M - 3B = M - \dfrac{3}{7}M = \dfrac{4}{7}M\).
Hence \(A = \dfrac{1}{7}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -4 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \dfrac{1}{7}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)
_note: Transcription flagged that the SAME matrix [[1,-1],[0,1]] is printed as the right-hand side of both equations (unlike sub-item (ii), which uses two distinct right-hand sides), raising a copy-paste suspicion. The book's own printed key resolves it: it gives A = (1/7)[[4,-4],[0,4]] and B = [[1/7,-1/7],[0,1/7]], which is exactly what two IDENTICAL right-hand sides produce. So the stem is as the book intends and the fractional sevenths are the book's own answer -- not a transcription defect. No change made.

solution:
Write \(P = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(Q = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(3A - B = P\) ... (1) and \(A + 5B = Q\) ... (2).
To eliminate \(B\), form \(5 \times (1) + (2)\): \(15A - 5B + A + 5B = 5P + Q\), that is \(16A = 5P + Q\).
\(5P + Q = \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 10 & 5 \\ 5 & 0 & 25 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 10 & 6 \\ 4 & 0 & 25 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(A = \dfrac{1}{16}\begin{bmatrix} -5 & 10 & 6 \\ 4 & 0 & 25 \end{bmatrix}\).
From (2), \(5B = Q - A = \dfrac{1}{16}\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -10 & 10 \\ -20 & 0 & -25 \end{bmatrix}\).
Hence \(A = \dfrac{1}{16}\begin{bmatrix} -5 & 10 & 6 \\ 4 & 0 & 25 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \dfrac{1}{16}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 & 2 \\ -4 & 0 & -5 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(B^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ 4 & -1 \\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(A + B^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -1 \\ 7 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and therefore
\((A + B^{T})^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 7 & 0 \\ -1 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
On the other side, \(A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & -1 \\ -3 & -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), so
\(A^{T} + 2B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 - 6 & 3 + 8 & -1 + 2 \\ -3 + 4 & -2 - 2 & 4 - 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 11 & 1 \\ 1 & -4 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\), which is NOT equal to \((A + B^{T})^{T}\).
The identity that does hold is \((A + B^{T})^{T} = A^{T} + (B^{T})^{T} = A^{T} + B\), and indeed
\(A^{T} + B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 - 3 & 3 + 4 & -1 + 1 \\ -3 + 2 & -2 - 1 & 4 - 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 7 & 0 \\ -1 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = (A + B^{T})^{T}\).
Hence the printed statement \((A + B^{T})^{T} = A^{T} + 2B\) is false; the correct result is \((A + B^{T})^{T} = A^{T} + B = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 7 & 0 \\ -1 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)
_note: Textbook misprint in the stem: it prints (A + B^T)^T = A^T + 2B. By the transpose rules (X + Y)^T = X^T + Y^T and (B^T)^T = B, the correct identity is A^T + B, and that is what the arithmetic gives. The coefficient 2 is likely carried over from sub-item (ii), where the 5 in 3A - 5B^T legitimately reappears in 3A^T - 5B. The matrix orders are consistent either way (both sides 2x3), so only the arithmetic exposes it. The book prints no key for this row (it omits verify questions), so there is no key to contradict. Solution verifies the CORRECT identity and states plainly that the printed one fails.

solution:
\(3A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -9 \\ 9 & -6 \\ -3 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(5B^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} -15 & 10 \\ 20 & -5 \\ 5 & -15 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(3A - 5B^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 21 & -19 \\ -11 & -1 \\ -8 & 27 \end{bmatrix}\).
Taking the transpose, L.H.S. \(= (3A - 5B^{T})^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 21 & -11 & -8 \\ -19 & -1 & 27 \end{bmatrix}\).
For the R.H.S., \(3A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 9 & -3 \\ -9 & -6 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(5B = \begin{bmatrix} -15 & 20 & 5 \\ 10 & -5 & -15 \end{bmatrix}\), so
\(3A^{T} - 5B = \begin{bmatrix} 21 & -11 & -8 \\ -19 & -1 & 27 \end{bmatrix}\).
Both sides are the same \(2 \times 3\) matrix, hence \((3A - 5B^{T})^{T} = 3A^{T} - 5B\) is verified.

\(A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\alpha & \sin\alpha \\ -\sin\alpha & \cos\alpha \end{bmatrix}\), so the off-diagonal sine terms cancel on addition:
\(A + A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 2\cos\alpha & 0 \\ 0 & 2\cos\alpha \end{bmatrix}\).
Equating this to \(I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) gives \(2\cos\alpha = 1\), that is \(\cos\alpha = \dfrac{1}{2}\).
Hence \(\alpha = 60^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\)

\(A\) is \(3 \times 2\) and \(B\) is \(2 \times 3\), so \(AB\) is a \(3 \times 3\) matrix.
\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 4 & -1 & -3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 1 & -4 \\ 11 & 7 & 0 \\ -1 & -3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\)
Expanding along the first row,
\(|AB| = 9(7 \times (-2) - 0 \times (-3)) - 1(11 \times (-2) - 0 \times (-1)) + (-4)(11 \times (-3) - 7 \times (-1))\)
\(= 9(-14) - 1(-22) - 4(-26) = -126 + 22 + 104 = 0\)
Since \(|AB| = 0\), \(AB\) is a singular matrix.

\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ -3 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -11 & 6 & -1 \\ -22 & 12 & -2 \\ -11 & 6 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\)
Here the third row is identical to the first row, so \(|AB| = 0\).
\(BA = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ -3 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\)
(for example the first row gives \(1 - 2 + 1 = 0\), \(2 - 4 + 2 = 0\), \(3 - 6 + 3 = 0\)), so \(|BA| = 0\) as well.
Since \(|AB| = 0\) and \(|BA| = 0\), both \(AB\) and \(BA\) are singular matrices.

\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 + 3 & 4 - 2 \\ 0 + 9 & 0 - 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 9 & -6 \end{bmatrix}\)
So \(|AB| = 5(-6) - 2(9) = -30 - 18 = -48\).
Also \(|A| = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 6 - 0 = 6\) and \(|B| = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -2 \end{vmatrix} = -2 - 6 = -8\), so \(|A||B| = 6 \times (-8) = -48\).
Hence \(|AB| = |A||B| = -48\), which verifies the result.

\(A_{\alpha} \cdot A_{\beta} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\alpha & \sin\alpha \\ -\sin\alpha & \cos\alpha \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \cos\beta & \sin\beta \\ -\sin\beta & \cos\beta \end{bmatrix}\)
\(= \begin{bmatrix} \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta & \cos\alpha\sin\beta + \sin\alpha\cos\beta \\ -\sin\alpha\cos\beta - \cos\alpha\sin\beta & -\sin\alpha\sin\beta + \cos\alpha\cos\beta \end{bmatrix}\)
Using the compound-angle formulae \(\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta\) and \(\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta\),
\(A_{\alpha} \cdot A_{\beta} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\alpha + \beta) & \sin(\alpha + \beta) \\ -\sin(\alpha + \beta) & \cos(\alpha + \beta) \end{bmatrix} = A_{\alpha + \beta}\)

Since \(\omega\) is a complex cube root of unity, \(\omega^{3} = 1\) and \(1 + \omega + \omega^{2} = 0\), so \(\omega^{2} + \omega = -1\), \(1 + \omega^{2} = -\omega\), \(1 + \omega = -\omega^{2}\) and \(\omega^{4} = \omega\).
\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} \omega^{2} + \omega & 1 + \omega^{2} \\ \omega^{4} + 1 & \omega^{2} + \omega \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -\omega \\ -\omega^{2} & -1 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(BA = \begin{bmatrix} \omega^{2} + \omega^{2} & \omega^{3} + 1 \\ 1 + \omega^{3} & \omega + \omega \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2\omega^{2} & 2 \\ 2 & 2\omega \end{bmatrix}\)
\(A - 2B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - 2\omega^{2} & \omega - 2 \\ \omega^{2} - 2 & 1 - 2\omega \end{bmatrix}\)
Adding the three matrices entry by entry:
\((1,1): -1 + 2\omega^{2} + 1 - 2\omega^{2} = 0\); \((1,2): -\omega + 2 + \omega - 2 = 0\); \((2,1): -\omega^{2} + 2 + \omega^{2} - 2 = 0\); \((2,2): -1 + 2\omega + 1 - 2\omega = 0\).
Hence \(AB + BA + A - 2B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), a null matrix.

\(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -5 \\ -4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -5 \\ -4 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 + 20 & -15 - 10 \\ -12 - 8 & 20 + 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 29 & -25 \\ -20 & 24 \end{bmatrix}\)
Also \(5A = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & -25 \\ -20 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(14I = \begin{bmatrix} 14 & 0 \\ 0 & 14 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(A^{2} - 5A - 14I = \begin{bmatrix} 29 - 15 - 14 & -25 + 25 - 0 \\ -20 + 20 - 0 & 24 - 10 - 14 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\)
Hence \(A^{2} - 5A - 14I = 0\).

\(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 + 1 & -2 - 2 \\ -2 - 2 & 1 + 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -4 \\ -4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\)
Also \(4A = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -4 \\ -4 & 8 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(3I = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(A^{2} - 4A + 3I = \begin{bmatrix} 5 - 8 + 3 & -4 + 4 + 0 \\ -4 + 4 + 0 & 5 - 8 + 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\)
Hence \(A^{2} - 4A + 3I = 0\).

Expanding, \((A + B)(A - B) = A^{2} - AB + BA - B^{2}\). So the given condition holds if and only if \(-AB + BA = 0\), that is \(AB = BA\).
\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & x \\ y & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 + 2y & -3x \\ 2 - 4y & 2x \end{bmatrix}\)
\(BA = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & x \\ y & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 + 2x & 2 - 4x \\ -3y & 2y \end{bmatrix}\)
Equating corresponding entries: from \((1,2)\), \(-3x = 2 - 4x\), so \(x = 2\); from \((2,1)\), \(2 - 4y = -3y\), so \(y = 2\). These also satisfy the remaining two entries, since \(-3 + 2y = -3 + 2x\) and \(2x = 2y\).
Hence \(x = 2\) and \(y = 2\)

\(A + B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(A - B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), so
\((A + B)(A - B) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).
On the other side, \(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\), so
\(A^{2} - B^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\).
Since \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \ne \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), we get \((A + B)(A - B) \ne A^{2} - B^{2}\). (The reason is that \(AB \ne BA\) here, so the cross terms do not cancel.)

First find \(A^{2}\):
\(A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 - 3 & -2 + 2 \\ 6 - 6 & -3 + 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I\)
Therefore \(A^{3} = A^{2} \cdot A = I \cdot A = A\).
Hence \(A^{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\)

First simplify the bracket:
\(2\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 3 & 6 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} + 3\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 10 \\ 6 & 12 \\ 4 & -2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 12 & 9 \\ 3 & 12 \\ 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 20 & 19 \\ 9 & 24 \\ 4 & -5 \end{bmatrix}\)
Now multiply by the row matrix:
\(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 20 & 19 \\ 9 & 24 \\ 4 & -5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 - 9 + 16 & 0 - 24 - 20 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & -44 \end{bmatrix}\)
Comparing with \(\begin{bmatrix} x & y \end{bmatrix}\), we get \(x = 7\), \(y = -44\)

First simplify the bracket:
\(-1\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} + 3\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 & 7 \\ 1 & -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -2 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -9 & 21 \\ 3 & -3 & 9 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -11 & 20 \\ 1 & -3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\)
Now multiply by the column matrix:
\(\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -11 & 20 \\ 1 & -3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 25 + 0 - 20 \\ 5 + 0 - 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\)
Comparing with \(\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}\), we get \(x = 5\), \(y = -1\)

First simplify the bracket:
\(5\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} - 3\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & -2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 5 \\ 5 & 0 \\ 5 & 5 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 3 \\ 9 & -6 \\ 3 & 9 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -6 & 2 \\ -4 & 6 \\ 2 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\)
Now multiply by the column matrix:
\(\begin{bmatrix} -6 & 2 \\ -4 & 6 \\ 2 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -12 + 2 \\ -8 + 6 \\ 4 - 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -10 \\ -2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\)
Equating with \(\begin{bmatrix} x - 1 \\ y + 1 \\ 2z \end{bmatrix}\): \(x - 1 = -10\), \(y + 1 = -2\), \(2z = 0\).
Hence \(x = -9\), \(y = -3\), \(z = 0\)

First simplify the bracket:
\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} + 2\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + 6 & 3 + 0 & 2 + 4 \\ 2 + 2 & 0 + 8 & 1 + 10 \\ 3 + 4 & 1 + 2 & 2 + 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 3 & 6 \\ 4 & 8 & 11 \\ 7 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\)
Now multiply by the column matrix:
\(\begin{bmatrix} 7 & 3 & 6 \\ 4 & 8 & 11 \\ 7 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 + 6 + 18 \\ 4 + 16 + 33 \\ 7 + 6 + 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 31 \\ 53 \\ 19 \end{bmatrix}\)
Comparing with \(\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}\), we get \(x = 31\), \(y = 53\), \(z = 19\)

\(B^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), and \(A\) is \(2 \times 3\), so \(AB^{T}\) is \(2 \times 2\):
\(AB^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 + 0 + 6 & 6 - 1 - 12 \\ 0 + 0 - 12 & 0 - 2 + 24 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -7 \\ -12 & 22 \end{bmatrix}\)
\(A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 \\ -3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\) is \(3 \times 2\) and \(B\) is \(2 \times 3\), so \(A^{T}B\) is \(3 \times 3\):
\(A^{T}B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 + 0 & 0 + 0 & -4 + 0 \\ 1 + 6 & 0 - 2 & -2 + 8 \\ -3 + 18 & 0 - 6 & 6 + 24 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & -4 \\ 7 & -2 & 6 \\ 15 & -6 & 30 \end{bmatrix}\)
Hence \(AB^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -7 \\ -12 & 22 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(A^{T}B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & -4 \\ 7 & -2 & 6 \\ 15 & -6 & 30 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -4 \\ 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 + 8 & -2 - 4 & 4 + 0 \\ 3 + 4 & -3 - 2 & 6 + 0 \\ 0 - 2 & 0 + 1 & 0 + 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & -6 & 4 \\ 7 & -5 & 6 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\)
So L.H.S. \(= (AB)^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 7 & -2 \\ -6 & -5 & 1 \\ 4 & 6 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\).
For the R.H.S., \(B^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & 0 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), so
\(B^{T}A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 + 8 & 3 + 4 & 0 - 2 \\ -2 - 4 & -3 - 2 & 0 + 1 \\ 4 + 0 & 6 + 0 & 0 + 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 7 & -2 \\ -6 & -5 & 1 \\ 4 & 6 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\)
Both sides are the same \(3 \times 3\) matrix, hence \((AB)^{T} = B^{T}A^{T}\).

Use induction on \(n\).
For \(n = 1\), the claimed matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 + 2 & -4 \\ 1 & 1 - 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = A\), so the result holds.
Assume it holds for \(n = k\), that is \(A^{k} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + 2k & -4k \\ k & 1 - 2k \end{bmatrix}\). Then
\(A^{k+1} = A^{k} \cdot A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + 2k & -4k \\ k & 1 - 2k \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 + 6k - 4k & -4 - 8k + 4k \\ 3k + 1 - 2k & -4k - 1 + 2k \end{bmatrix}\)
\(= \begin{bmatrix} 3 + 2k & -4 - 4k \\ k + 1 & -1 - 2k \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + 2(k+1) & -4(k+1) \\ k + 1 & 1 - 2(k+1) \end{bmatrix}\),
which is the claimed form for \(n = k + 1\).
Hence by the principle of mathematical induction, \(A^{n} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + 2n & -4n \\ n & 1 - 2n \end{bmatrix}\) for all \(n \in N\).

Use induction on \(n\).
For \(n = 1\), the claimed matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix} = A\), so the result holds.
Assume it holds for \(n = k\), that is \(A^{k} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos k\theta & \sin k\theta \\ -\sin k\theta & \cos k\theta \end{bmatrix}\). Then
\(A^{k+1} = A^{k} \cdot A = \begin{bmatrix} \cos k\theta\cos\theta - \sin k\theta\sin\theta & \cos k\theta\sin\theta + \sin k\theta\cos\theta \\ -\sin k\theta\cos\theta - \cos k\theta\sin\theta & -\sin k\theta\sin\theta + \cos k\theta\cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\)
Using \(\cos(k\theta + \theta) = \cos k\theta\cos\theta - \sin k\theta\sin\theta\) and \(\sin(k\theta + \theta) = \sin k\theta\cos\theta + \cos k\theta\sin\theta\),
\(A^{k+1} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(k+1)\theta & \sin(k+1)\theta \\ -\sin(k+1)\theta & \cos(k+1)\theta \end{bmatrix}\), which is the claimed form for \(n = k + 1\).
Hence by the principle of mathematical induction, \(A^{n} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos n\theta & \sin n\theta \\ -\sin n\theta & \cos n\theta \end{bmatrix}\) for all \(n \in N\).

Write the two months' sales as matrices with rows Shantaram, Kantaram and columns rice, wheat, groundnut. The total for the two months is their sum.
\(\begin{bmatrix} 15000 & 13000 & 12000 \\ 18000 & 15000 & 8000 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 18000 & 15000 & 12000 \\ 21000 & 16500 & 16000 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 33000 & 28000 & 24000 \\ 39000 & 31500 & 24000 \end{bmatrix}\)
So the total sale for the two months is:

| Total sale (Rs.) | Rice | Wheat | Groundnut |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shantaram | 33000 | 28000 | 24000 |
| Kantaram | 39000 | 31500 | 24000 |

Hence Shantaram: rice Rs. 33000, wheat Rs. 28000, groundnut Rs. 24000; Kantaram: rice Rs. 39000, wheat Rs. 31500, groundnut Rs. 24000.

The increase from April to May is the May matrix minus the April matrix (rows Shantaram, Kantaram; columns rice, wheat, groundnut).
\(\begin{bmatrix} 18000 & 15000 & 12000 \\ 21000 & 16500 & 16000 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 15000 & 13000 & 12000 \\ 18000 & 15000 & 8000 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3000 & 2000 & 0 \\ 3000 & 1500 & 8000 \end{bmatrix}\)
So the increase in sale is:

| Increase (Rs.) | Rice | Wheat | Groundnut |
|---|---|---|---|
